name: PT Sawit Sumbermas Sarana Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Sawit Sumbermas Sarana: a deep-discount palm cash flow and the discount that explains it
frontmatter.summary: Sawit Sumbermas Sarana is a Central Kalimantan palm producer whose shares trade at a deep discount to our estimate of fundamental value, because the name sits on the exchange's high-concentration list and inside MSCI's standalone consultation. The plantation earns real cash at deck prices, pays a large dividend and is de-levering. We rate BUY: the target assumes only part of the discount closes over twelve months.
thesis: The shares trade at 0.44 times today's fundamental value of Rp2,196, against a twelve-month fundamental value of Rp2,425 [S0, S22, S24].
Nine-month parent profit rose 58.4% on revenue growth of 34.9%, and the run-rate supports a forward dividend above the FY2025 payout [S7, S12].

Leverage is serviceable on the forecast path: net debt is 1.7x FY2026E EBITDA at the FY2026E year-end, though the 30 September balance sheet already carries IDR11,125.3bn of net debt, and the restricted DHE balance is debt-funded and excluded from cash [S7, F46, F101].
The discount is market structure, not earnings: HSC membership [S22], MSCI's standalone consultation [S24], and a 62.3% controller with a thin residual free float [S0].
Our Rp1,330 target keeps only 25.0% of the log gap closed in the base regime case, a total return of 53.1% [S22, S24].

catalysts.event: Cum-interim-dividend date in the regular and negotiated market
Exchange review of the high-shareholding-concentration list; SSMS is currently on it
FY2026 audited results, following the FY2025 accounts published on 1 April 2026
MSCI final decision on reclassifying Indonesia to standalone market status
Final free-float step under the exchange's free-float rule; SSMS is above it on the registry measure, with the residual after the controlling block as the sensitivity

blocks.text: **BUY; twelve-month target Rp1,330, a total return of 53.1% from Rp960.** The target is not a statement that the plantation is worth a multiple of the market price. It is the engine's konglo lens saying that a share of today's discount is likely to close over the next twelve months, while most of it stays in place. Fundamental value on a twelve-month view is Rp2,425; today's fundamental value is Rp2,196, so the market is paying 0.44 times what the business is worth to a control buyer, and the lens keeps a probability-weighted share of that gap [S0, S22, S24]. We rate the shares BUY because the cash flow alone, at the deck's own CPO path, supports a value well above the price even after the discount is only partly closed.

What the company owns is a Central Kalimantan palm platform: 23 estates covering 115,584 ha, 10 mills, a kernel crushing plant and a biogas unit, all feeding a product slate of crude palm oil, RBD palm olein, crude palm kernel oil and palm kernel [S4, S14, S19]. In FY2025 the group processed 2,382,942 t of fresh fruit bunches, produced 527,052 t of CPO at an oil extraction rate of 22.1%, and sold enough volume to generate revenue of IDR14,810.0bn and parent profit of IDR1,160.0bn [S14, S8]. Nine months into FY2026 revenue had already reached IDR14,830.0bn and parent profit IDR1,590.0bn, both well ahead of the comparable period [S7].

The variant view is about the price of the equity, not the quality of the estate. SSMS is a profitable, dividend-paying upstream producer whose shares trade at a fraction of what its cash flows support. The reason is ownership and index structure: the company is 62.3% controlled by PT Citra Borneo Indah, the exchange has placed the stock on its high-shareholding-concentration list [S22], and the registry free float of 29.2% leaves only a thin residual once the controlling block is set aside [S25, S0]. On top of that, MSCI has opened a consultation to reclassify Indonesia as a standalone market, with a final decision due by the end of June 2027 and a freeze on index increases in the meantime [S24]. For a name whose marginal buyer is an index or a flow, those are direct hits to the multiple rather than to the cash flow.

The cash flow is real and improving. Nine-month revenue rose 34.9% and parent profit 58.4%, with gross profit of IDR5,950.0bn and operating profit of IDR2,760.0bn [S7]. The company paid IDR800.0bn of dividends for FY2025, a payout of 68.9%, and has already declared a IDR500.0bn interim dividend for FY2026 [S12, S3]. Leverage is not comfortable but it is serviceable: our FY2026E net debt to EBITDA is 1.7x at the FY2026E year-end, falling to 1.0x in FY2027E as cash builds [S0]. The current position is heavier than that path: net debt was IDR11,125.3bn at 30 September 2026, against the FY2025A year-end line of IDR7,549.1bn [S7, F101]. The catch is that the balance sheet carries a IDR3,200.0bn restricted DHE balance that is debt-funded and cannot be spent, so headline assets overstate liquidity [S7].

Three things move the value. The first is the CPO price: the house agri deck (fund record d.agri.cpo) runs from US$1,135/t in FY2026E to US$1,240/t in FY2027E, against a long-run marker of US$1,150/t, and the engine's reverse DCF shows today's price already discounts US$1,146/t, below the deck. The second is whether the discount closes at all: the free-float rule is not the binding constraint for SSMS, so the regime catalyst is the HSC and MSCI track rather than a forced sell-down [S25, S24]. The third is the SML integration: the 11,046 ha estate bought from the controlling shareholder for IDR1,600.0bn consolidates with a 63.4% stake, so a rising minority share takes part of the group's profit growth away from parent shareholders [S5, S13, S7].

The construction is explicit because it is easy to misread. The method blend gives Rp2,332 a share today; rolling that forward at the cost of equity and deducting the next-twelve-month dividend gives a base-case value of Rp2,581; probability-weighting the business scenarios gives Rp2,425; and after the liquidity discount the fundamental twelve-month value is Rp2,425 (engine, valuation chain). The konglo lens then applies the regime layer: the base regime case gives Rp1,304, the bear Rp898 and the bull Rp1,815; weighted at one quarter, one half and one quarter, the target is Rp1,330, which is the ratio of the target to the Rp2,425 fundamental value applied to today's log discount. That ratio is just over half (Rp1,330 against Rp2,425), not the base regime's closing share, and the arithmetic is transparent rather than a shorthand [S22, S24].

The honest caveat is that the target is a bet on the discount, not on the trees. If the exchange keeps SSMS on the concentration list and MSCI proceeds to standalone status, the discount can persist and the shares can stay cheap for years; the bear regime case values them at Rp898, below the current price [S22, S24]. If instead the group addresses the structure, the bull regime case reaches Rp1,815 [S24]. We weight the base case at half because the direction of the regime is clear but the timing is not.

PT Sawit Sumbermas Sarana Tbk is an oil-palm plantation and milling company based in Pangkalan Bun, Central Kalimantan, founded in 1995 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2013 [S19]. It is a subsidiary of PT Citra Borneo Indah, which holds 62.3% of the shares, and it sits inside the Citra Borneo Indah group [S19, S13]. The operating footprint is a single province: nucleus estates, plasma smallholder blocks and third-party fruit all converge on the company's own mills in Central Kalimantan, so there is geographic concentration as well as ownership concentration [S13, S11].

The asset base is larger than the profile pages suggest. At the October 2025 extraordinary meeting the company operated 23 estates covering 115,584 ha, supported by mills with combined capacity of 540 t/h, a kernel crushing plant of 180 t/day and a biogas plant [S4]. By the FY2025 operating disclosure the mill count had risen to 10, reflecting the consolidation of the SML estate and its facilities [S14, S13]. The estate profile is a mix of mature nucleus blocks and younger plantings, and the SML acquisition was explicitly justified by the age of its palms: management described the acquired area as dominated by young trees that would add production over the medium term [S4, S5].

The volume chain is disclosed in unusual detail for an Indonesian mid-cap. In FY2025 the company produced 1,628,452 t of nucleus FFB and processed 2,382,942 t in total, sourcing the balance from plasma blocks (44,400 t) and third-party growers (516,000 t) [S14, S11]. That 516,000 t of purchased fruit is roughly a fifth of throughput: SSMS is not a pure estate play but a mill system that also competes for other people's fruit, which supports utilisation and dilutes estate risk [S11]. Output was 527,052 t of CPO, 104,130 t of palm kernel and 15,379 t of palm kernel oil, at an extraction rate of 22.1% and CPO production growth of 14.2% [S14].

The product slate runs from crude palm oil into a small downstream step. The company sells CPO and its derivatives, specifically RBD palm olein, crude palm kernel oil and palm kernel, to third-party buyers across export and domestic markets, with third-party sales dominating the customer mix [S7, S2]. The archive does not carry a product-level revenue split, so we do not claim one; what is clear is that the revenue line is a commodity price line, and the FY2025 revenue growth of 43.0% on flat-to-modest volume was a price and currency event rather than a volume event [S8, S14].

The strategy is upstream expansion plus sustainability credentials. The company bought 98,328 SML shares from its parent for IDR1,600.0bn in a transaction completed on 24 November 2025, lifting its stake to 63.4% and leaving CBI with 36.5% [S13, S5]. The purchase was funded from a syndicated facility of up to IDR5,200.0bn led by Bank Rakyat Indonesia with seven other lenders, signed on 18 November 2025, which also refinances existing debt and funds estate development, infrastructure and working capital [S13, S4]. Operationally the company has invested in extraction efficiency and traceability, reporting full ISPO and RSPO certification and a traceable supply chain of 2,000,000 t of FFB [S11, S21].

Market position is mid-tier. On FY2025 revenue SSMS is the fifth-largest listed palm producer, behind the Sinar Mas, Astra Agro, Tunas Baru Lampung and Salim Ivomas platforms, and it is an order of magnitude smaller than the leader, whose net sales were IDR86,950.0bn against SSMS's IDR14,810.0bn [S10]. That matters for the investment case: SSMS is a price-taker with no meaningful influence on the CPO benchmark, and it does not have the downstream refining and oleochemical integration that lets the largest peers capture a second margin [S10, S12].

Palm oil is the most heavily traded vegetable oil in the world. The tree produces two distinct streams from the same fruit: crude palm oil from the mesocarp and palm kernel oil from the kernel, with palm kernel meal as a by-product. Fresh fruit bunches must be milled within a day or two of harvest, so estates and mills are always co-located and transport radius is a hard constraint on scale. Yields improve as palms mature, peak in the middle years and decline thereafter, which is why planters talk about age profiles and replanting as much as about acreage. Indonesia and Malaysia dominate global supply, and Indonesian producers sell into both the domestic food market and the export market, so the rupiah, the export levy and the domestic price reference all interact.

The palm complex is a price cycle with a policy overlay, and both matter for SSMS. The house deck prices CPO at US$1,007/t for FY2025A, rising to US$1,135/t in FY2026E and US$1,240/t in FY2027E before easing to US$1,210/t and a long-run marker of US$1,150/t (fund record d.agri.cpo). That shape is not a straight-line bull case: it assumes a tight middle of the decade driven by biodiesel demand and slow replanting, followed by normalisation as supply responds. The spot print at the time of writing is US$1,180/t, below the FY2027E deck number, and the archive shows CPO falling for four consecutive sessions to a twenty-five-week low in early November 2026 [S16]. Our forecasts use the deck, not the spot, and the sensitivity table shows the cost of being wrong.

Demand is the part of the story the company can rely on least and the market relies on most. The company's own outlook points to rising global vegetable-oil demand from population growth, food-industry expansion and alternative energy, and the Indonesian biodiesel mandate is the single largest policy support for palm demand [S12, S16]. Supply is the offsetting force: ageing trees across the Indonesian and Malaysian estates mean the incremental tonne is expensive, and the industry's replanting deficit is now a multi-year constraint [S12, S10]. The deck's hump-and-normalise path is our way of holding both: tight near term, looser later (fund record d.agri.cpo).

Policy is a direct tax on the revenue line. Indonesia's export levy and duty are embedded in the realisation wedge we apply, so the government takes a slice of every exported tonne before the producer sees it, and the domestic-market obligation reallocates part of the crop to local buyers at administered reference prices [S11, S16]. That is why the model carries a flat realisation of 0.95 against the benchmark rather than assuming a product premium: the olein and kernel products earn a little more, and the levy, duty and freight take a little more, and we hold the net wedge constant rather than forecast its direction [S0]. On top of the fiscal layer sits the sustainability regime: ISPO is mandatory for Indonesian producers, RSPO is the export-market credential, and European traceability requirements have made supply-chain documentation a condition of access rather than a marketing extra [S11, S13].

The competitive landscape is fragmented at the small end and concentrated at the top. Among listed producers, the five largest by FY2025 revenue are the Sinar Mas, Astra Agro, Tunas Baru Lampung, Salim Ivomas and SSMS platforms, and the leaders' advantage is downstream integration: the producers that refine, fractionate and sell branded products capture a second margin that a pure CPO seller does not [S10]. SSMS sits at the upstream end with a small olein and kernel oil step, so its margin is a spread between the CPO benchmark and its cash cost, and its returns are more cyclical than the integrated peers' [S10, S7]. That is visible in the history: EBITDA margin fell to 10.6% in the FY2023 trough and recovered to 20.3% in FY2025 [S0].

The moat is real but narrow. The company's extraction rate of 22.1% is a genuine operational advantage in a business where a point of OER is worth several percent of revenue, and full ISPO and RSPO certification with traceability across 2,000,000 t of fruit is a licence to sell into premium export markets that uncertified smallholders do not have [S14, S11]. The mill network and the 516,000 t of third-party fruit show that SSMS is a preferred processor for surrounding growers, which supports utilisation beyond its own estate [S11]. What the company does not have is a cost-curve position: we hold no sourced public cost curve that would let us place SSMS in a global quartile, and we will not claim one [S4]. The honest summary is that the moat is asset quality and certification, not pricing power.

The five forces point to a middling industry. Buyer power is high because CPO is fungible and priced off a benchmark, although certification narrows the buyer set for premium volumes [S11]. Supplier power is moderate and rising: third-party fruit is a fifth of throughput, and those growers have alternatives, so the company competes for supply in a tight replanting environment [S11, S10]. Barriers to entry are high at the permit and mill level and low at the smallholder level, which is exactly the structure that keeps returns cyclical [S12]. Substitution risk runs through soybean, sunflower and rapeseed oil, and the price spread among them is what makes palm demand elastic at the margin (fund record d.agri.soyoil). Rivalry is intense among Indonesian and Malaysian producers selling into the same export markets [S10].

Currency is the quiet driver. SSMS earns in dollar-linked CPO revenue and pays most of its cost base in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah flatters the margin. The deck has USD/IDR at Rp17,570/USD for FY2026E and Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E against a spot of Rp18,190/USD, and the model converts revenue at the deck rate while escalating rupiah costs with domestic inflation [S0]. That is a tailwind in the forecast, not a hedge: a stronger rupiah would compress the spread just as the CPO cycle turns (fund record m.usd_idr).

The five-year record is a cycle, not a trend. Revenue was IDR11,240.2bn in FY2022, slipped to IDR10,703.4bn and IDR10,366.8bn as CPO normalised, then jumped to IDR14,810.0bn in FY2025, a gain of 43.0% [S0, S8]. EBITDA followed the same path and then some: IDR1,136.3bn in the trough, IDR1,934.8bn in FY2024 and IDR3,004.4bn in FY2025, when the margin reached 20.3% [S0]. Parent profit went from IDR1,837.4bn to IDR512.3bn, recovered to IDR819.5bn and reached IDR1,160.0bn [S0]. The FY2023 trough is the number that matters for risk: net debt to EBITDA hit 6.2x that year on FY2023's own net debt, but the 30 September 2026 net debt of IDR11,125.3bn against the same trough EBITDA of IDR1,136.3bn is close to ten times, and even the FY2025A year-end line of IDR7,549.1bn is already a higher multiple than the FY2023 figure, so a repeat of that cycle would leave the balance sheet at a materially higher multiple [S0, S7, F101].

The FY2025 accounts are the anchor for the model. Revenue of IDR14,810.0bn carried gross profit of IDR5,170.0bn and group net profit of IDR1,200.0bn, of which IDR1,160.0bn was attributable to the parent, or Rp122 a share [S8, S10]. The year-on-year growth rates were 42.0% at the net profit line, 42.0% at the parent line and 58.0% at gross profit, all driven by price rather than volume: CPO output rose 14.2% and nucleus FFB 4.2% [S10, S14]. The balance sheet expanded 14.0% to IDR13,600.0bn of assets, while total equity grew only 1.9% to IDR2,940.0bn and cash fell 26.0% to IDR874.0bn, the signature of a year in which growth was funded by debt rather than retained cash [S8].

FY2026 is running ahead of that base on revenue, but not on margin. Nine-month revenue of IDR14,830.0bn was 34.9% higher, cost of revenue rose to IDR8,890.0bn, and gross profit rose to IDR5,950.0bn [S7, S2]. Operating profit reached IDR2,760.0bn, up 43.1%, pre-tax profit IDR2,330.0bn, up 52.2%, and the tax charge IDR575.1bn, up from IDR396.8bn [S7, S2]. Group net profit was IDR1,750.0bn, up 71.3%, and parent profit IDR1,590.0bn, up 58.4% [S7]. The gap between group and parent profit is the minority share, and it widened as SML consolidated at a 63.4% ownership [S7, S5].

The forecast is built from that nine-month actual, not from the FY2025 year, because the cost lines moved with the price. Nine-month revenue of IDR14,830.0bn less cost of revenue of IDR8,890.0bn less operating profit of IDR2,760.0bn leaves SG&A and selling cost at 21.4% of revenue, and cost of revenue less D&A on the same volume gives a cash cost of IDR10.7m a tonne. We carry both ratios into the fourth quarter unchanged, so FY2026E revenue of IDR19,797.4bn and EBITDA of IDR4,321.2bn give a margin of 21.8%, the same margin the nine-month accounts show, with no fourth-quarter step-up assumed. That is deliberately not the FY2025 cost base: the FY2025 year earned a lower SG&A ratio and a lower cash cost, and applying it to the FY2026 price would have produced a margin the company has not delivered [S7, F32, F37, F40].

The revenue build in our model is volume times realisation times the benchmark, and the volume is the least visible input in the pack. The data pack carries no volume history, so we derived the FY2025 trading volume from the revenue line: IDR14,810.0bn divided by the FY2025 CPO benchmark, the average exchange rate and the realisation wedge implies 941 kt of CPO-equivalent sales [F59]. That is turnover, not output. The disclosed physical chain gives own CPO production of 527,052 t, palm kernel of 104,130 t and palm kernel oil of 15,379 t, which is product output well below the modelled sales; the balance, roughly a third of the modelled volume, is product the company buys and resells. The archive does not disclose that trading flow separately, so we say so rather than dress it up: the 941 kt modelled sales figure is CPO-equivalent turnover including resale, and the company's own output does not reconcile to it. Both F59 and F60 are derived, not separately disclosed, and the 0.95 realisation is the actual-implied wedge to the FY2025 benchmark, not a forecast haircut. Because volume and realisation are jointly identified from the revenue line, we anchor the pair to the actual year rather than to a peer's product mix [F59][F60][S10]. The archive carries no product-level revenue split and no levy schedule, so the wedge cannot be decomposed into product premium, export levy, duty and freight; we hold it at the revenue-implied level rather than importing a peer's lower realisation, which reflects a different product mix and would require a different volume to reproduce the same revenue. This is a joint identification, not a calibration of each leg, and the calibration gate validates the EBITDA level rather than the split. Because revenue is the product of the two, a given percentage change in either moves revenue by the same amount, and the volume axis of the sensitivity table prices that risk. We carry the volume base forward at 1,045.0kt in FY2026E and 1,090.0kt in FY2027E, lifting it as the SML palms mature and then flattening as the young-planting uplift annualises [S4, S7].

Cost is where the model had to be rebuilt. The pack's depreciation line is the G&A-only charge, not group D&A: the FY2025 cash-flow identity, operating cash flow less net profit plus the working-capital build, implies D&A of about IDR568.3bn, or roughly IDR0.6m a tonne, and the same identity for FY2024 gives IDR294.5bn [S0, F60, F98]. Using the pack line would have understated EBITDA by that gap in both years and made every multiple look expensive. We restate D&A for the last two fiscal years and set the cash cost from the nine-month actual rather than from the FY2025 year: the FY2025 base no longer reproduces the run-rate once the 9M2026 cost of revenue and D&A are taken out, so the FY2026 cash cost is anchored on the filing and then escalated [S7, F40, F60, F98]. The resulting cash cost is about IDR10.7m a tonne in FY2026E, escalating with rupiah inflation, with the purchased-feed share of throughput, 23.5%, treated as the slice of the cost base whose price tracks the CPO benchmark [S11, S14].

That cost structure is why the margin widens with the deck rather than staying flat. Only the purchased-feed share of throughput is bought fruit, so a higher CPO price lifts revenue much more than it lifts cost; the remaining own-estate cost moves with rupiah inflation. Our FY2026E EBITDA margin is 21.8% and FY2027E is 26.4%, against 20.3% in FY2025, as the deck's CPO price rises from US$1,135/t to US$1,240/t [S0, F60]. SG&A is held at 21.4% of revenue, the nine-month FY2026 level, because the selling and export costs that rose with the price are unlikely to fall as fast, and the lower FY2025 ratio was earned at a lower price [S7, S8].

Cash conversion is decent but not clean. FY2025 operating cash flow covered net profit only after adding back the working-capital build of IDR673.8bn, and operating working capital ended the year at IDR3,178.9bn, or 22.6% of revenue [S0]. That is a high working-capital intensity for a commodity producer and it is the main reason free cash flow of IDR1,179.9bn sat below EBITDA [S0]. We carry the same ratio forward, which means growth absorbs cash: the FY2026E working-capital build is IDR1,286.6bn on revenue of IDR19,797.4bn [S0].

Capex is rising with the acquisition and the mill programme. FY2025 capex was IDR475.1bn; we forecast IDR731.5bn in FY2026E and IDR782.1bn in FY2027E as SML development, replanting and infrastructure are funded from the syndicated facility [S13, S0]. That is about IDR0.7m a tonne, well below the long-run EBITDA line, so the capex gate is not a constraint on the valuation [S0]. Free cash flow to the firm is IDR1,380.5bn in FY2026E and IDR3,199.7bn in FY2027E, which is what the DCF capitalises [S0].

The balance sheet is the weak point. Gross debt was IDR8,423.1bn at the FY2025A year-end and net debt IDR7,549.1bn, rising to a year-end FY2026E gross figure of IDR9,323.1bn as the SML purchase and the dividend were funded with borrowings [S0, S13]. Net debt to EBITDA is 1.7x in FY2026E and 1.0x in FY2027E, but those are year-end forecast lines and not the current position. The DCF deducts the 30 September 2026 net debt of IDR11,125.3bn, which is IDR7,549.1bn plus the increase in borrowings since the FY2025A year-end, and it is close to ten times the FY2023 trough EBITDA of IDR1,136.3bn, against the 6.2x struck on FY2023's own, much lower net debt [S7, F101]. The September balance sheet already carries more debt than the year-end forecast, so the forecast path is optimistic on deleveraging; the DCF uses the September net debt, not the forecast line [S7, F101]. But the September balance sheet shows current liabilities of IDR9,480.0bn against current assets of IDR11,100.0bn and total liabilities of IDR15,100.0bn against IDR18,710.0bn of assets, and the current assets include the IDR3,200.0bn restricted DHE balance that cannot be used to repay anything [S7]. Strip that out and liquidity is thinner than the headline suggests.

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly and slightly aggressive at the same time. The company paid IDR800.0bn for FY2025, a 68.9% payout, retained IDR360.7bn and has declared a IDR500.0bn interim dividend for FY2026, equal to Rp52 a share, payable on 2 December 2026 [S12, S3]. Paying out at that rate while gross debt rises is a choice to keep the yield high and the register loyal; it is defensible at current cash generation but it removes the buffer a cyclical producer usually keeps [S0, S7]. The unrestricted retained earnings balance of IDR3,040.0bn is the constraint on how far the payout can go under Indonesian company law [S3].

We flag six earnings-quality issues. First, the reported depreciation line is not group D&A, and using it would overstate the multiple; we restate it from the cash-flow identity and disclose the derivation [S0, F60]. Second, the minority share of profit is rising with the SML consolidation, so group profit growth overstates what reaches parent shareholders [S7, F34, F36]. Third, working capital absorbs a large share of incremental revenue, so EBITDA is a weaker proxy for cash than usual [S0]. Fourth, the restricted DHE balance inflates total assets and flatters the current ratio without adding liquidity [S7, F46]. Fifth, the SML purchase was an affiliate transaction with the controlling shareholder, priced at IDR1,600.0bn and funded with debt, which transfers value between related parties rather than discovering a market price [S13, S5]. Sixth, the effective tax rate runs above the statutory rate because of local taxes and levies, and we hold 25.0% rather than the statutory rate [S7].

Our forecast lands at revenue of IDR19,797.4bn in FY2026E and IDR23,561.8bn in FY2027E, EBITDA of IDR4,321.2bn and IDR6,216.2bn, and parent profit of IDR2,040.5bn and IDR3,291.9bn [S0]. That is Rp214 of earnings per share in FY2026E against Rp122 in FY2025, with dividends of Rp139 and Rp225 on a 65.0% payout [S0]. Return on equity is 70.4%, which looks spectacular and is mostly leverage: parent equity is thin relative to revenue, and the return is the reward for the balance-sheet risk described above [S0].

A plantation is a depleting, price-taking asset, so we value it on a discounted cash flow at through-cycle prices, cross-checked on EV/EBITDA and P/BV. The primary method is a ten-year FCFF model discounted at a bottom-up cost of capital, with a Gordon terminal value at 4.0% nominal. The discount rate is built from the house macro deck (fund record) and the industry beta in operating configuration rather than assumed: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, an unlevered industry beta of 0.80 and a cost of debt of 9.4% pre-tax, blended at the model's gearing.

At a WACC of 11.4% and a cost of equity of 16.7%, the DCF gives Rp2,963 a share, with enterprise value of IDR40,275.2bn and terminal value 49.8% of the total (engine, method dcf_fcff). The high terminal share is the honest weakness of the method: it capitalises a perpetual spread between the CPO deck and the cost base, and it is sensitive to the long-run price assumption in the house agri deck (fund record d.agri.cpo). We keep the DCF as primary because it is the only method that captures the volume ramp, the rising dividend and the deleveraging path, and we cross-check it rather than rely on it.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check at 8.8 times gives Rp1,504, -49.3% below the DCF, and the P/BV cross-check at 3.7 times gives Rp1,184, -60.0% below it (engine, methods ev_ebitda and pbv). We do not treat those gaps as evidence that the DCF is wrong. The EV/EBITDA multiple is anchored on a stale earnings base: it is applied to FY2025A EBITDA of IDR3,004.4bn, the last audited year, which is well below the FY2026E run-rate of IDR4,321.2bn; on the forward number the same multiple would land close to the DCF. The own-history component of that multiple is also computed on the pack's reported EBITDA, which carries the G&A-only depreciation line, so it is inflated: on the restated D&A the own five-year average falls by roughly a quarter and the blended multiple of 8.8 by roughly a sixth, which would cut the EV/EBITDA leg by about a fortieth of the blended value. That is small against the gap to the DCF but it is not nothing, and it is the reason we do not lean on the multiple. The P/BV multiple is applied to the restated parent book of IDR3,076.8bn at 30 September 2026, which is total equity of IDR3,610.0bn less minority interests on the same 30 September balance sheet, not the stale June parent book the pack carries [S7, S0].

The P/BV leg deserves a second caveat: the own-history component of the multiple average embeds the same concentrated-ownership discount that the konglo lens is designed to measure separately. Applying a discount-era multiple to current book value double-counts the discount, which is why the P/BV value sits so far below the DCF [S22, S24]. The leg is IDR3,076.8bn of parent book at 30 September 2026 times 3.7, or Rp1,184 a share; the pack's June parent book is lower and would understate the leg. We keep the method because the house card requires it as a cross-check, but we weight it at 15.0% and treat the DCF as the value anchor.

Weighting the DCF at 60.0%, EV/EBITDA at 25.0% and P/BV at 15.0% gives Rp2,332 a share today [S0]. Rolling that forward twelve months at the cost of equity and deducting the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp139 gives a base-case value of Rp2,581; probability-weighting the bear, base and bull business scenarios gives Rp2,425; and applying the 0.0% liquidity discount leaves a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp2,425 (engine, valuation chain). The liquidity discount is zero because the exchange's IDX-IC registry free float of 29.2% is above the minimum threshold the rule tests, and the stock's three-month average daily turnover is IDR11.3bn; the discount that matters here is the regime discount, which the lens prices separately [S25, S0]. The chain matters: Rp2,581 is the base case alone, Rp2,425 is the probability-weighted business value, and Rp2,425 is that value after the liquidity adjustment.

The bridge is explicit about the balance-sheet claims. The DCF capitalises the consolidated group, so we deduct net debt and minority interests, both at 30 September 2026. The engine adds the associates as an investment and the bridge removes the same investments line again, because the associate contribution is already inside the operating result; the net effect is nil, so the associate is neither double counted nor omitted, and both legs now use the same September balance-sheet date. The minority is deducted on a capitalised basis: the SML acquisition price of IDR1,600.0bn for 63.4% implies a value for the minority stake (the complement of that holding) above its book carrying value, and we deduct that excess on top of the September book minority. Both adjustments sit in valuation.bridge and are sourced to the pack and the SML transaction [S0, S5, F16].

The asset-value cross-check points the same way. The SML transaction valued 11,046 ha at IDR1,600.0bn for a 63.4% stake, which implies a per-hectare value that, applied to SSMS's 115,584 ha, puts the land alone at IDR26,407.5bn, several times the IDR9,144.0bn market capitalisation. We do not use that as the primary value because the estate is a going concern with a finite tree life, but it is a floor under the bear case and it explains why the SML price is both a governance risk and an asset marker [S5, S13, F10, F14, F16]. The dividend-capacity anchor is the other cross-check: at the modeled payout the shares yield 14.5% in FY2026E and 23.4% in FY2027E, well above the through-cycle cost of equity, which is the market's alternative anchor [S0, S12]. On reserve life, the company does not disclose a stand-alone reserve; as a perennial tree crop with replanting, we use the explicit forecast horizon plus a terminal value rather than a depleting reserve life [S4, S14].

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of what the market believes. At Rp960 the engine's reverse DCF solves for a FY2027E CPO price of US$1,146/t, or 92.4% of the house agri deck's US$1,240/t (fund record d.agri.cpo). In other words, the market is not paying for the deck's cycle at all; it is paying for a below-deck cycle and a persistent discount on top. That is consistent with the multiples: 4.5x FY2026E earnings, 4.0x EV/EBITDA, 2.6x book and a 14.5% dividend yield are not plantation multiples, they are discount multiples [S0].

Now the konglo lens, which is what turns fundamental value into a target. The lens measures the price against today's probability-weighted fundamental value of Rp2,196 and finds the shares at 0.44 times it: a discount, not a premium [S22, S24]. It then assumes that a share of the log gap closes over twelve months, with the share set by the name's regime flags. SSMS carries the high-shareholding-concentration flag, which cuts the closing share by 5.0% because the name is below fundamental value, and it does not carry the free-float flag: the exchange's IDX-IC registry measures the free float at 29.2%, above the minimum the rule tests, so no free-float step is due inside the window. The pack's insider and institution fields overlap rather than partition the register, so the residual after the controlling block is thinner than the registry number; we show that residual as a sensitivity rather than as the compliance measure [S25, S22, S0]. In the base regime case 25.0% of the log gap closes, in the bear case the discount widens by -20.0% of the log gap, and in the bull case 65.0% closes [S22, S24].

Applied to the twelve-month fundamental value, the base regime case gives Rp1,304, the bear case Rp898 and the bull case Rp1,815 [S22, S24]. Probability-weighted at one quarter, one half and one quarter, the lens produces our Rp1,330 target, a total return of 53.1% (engine, konglo lens). Note what the target is not: it is not Rp2,425 and it is certainly not the DCF's Rp2,963. It is the value of the business after assuming that most of the discount survives the year.

We are deliberately conservative on the closure rate. The exchange's HSC list is reviewed periodically and SSMS has no announced plan to lift its float or restructure its ownership; the free-float rule does not force it to act; and MSCI's consultation points toward reclassification rather than resolution [S22, S25, S24]. A company that does nothing can stay on the list indefinitely. The counter-case is that the group has already shown willingness to simplify: it bought SML from the parent and has kept a high payout, which suggests the controlling family values the listed vehicle [S13, S12]. That is why the bull case gets a quarter, not zero.

What would make us change the method? A sustained CPO price above the house deck would lift fundamental value without touching the discount, and the sensitivity table shows the effect; a structural fix to the ownership or index status would collapse the discount and make the lens unnecessary; and a deterioration in the balance sheet would make the DCF, not the discount, the binding constraint [S7]. None of those is our base case.

The largest risk is that the discount is not a temporary mispricing but the market's correct price for a structure that does not change. SSMS is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list published on 22 October 2026, and HSC names leave the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026, so the passive bid is gone as well as the active one [S22, S26]. MSCI has frozen index increases for Indonesian securities while it consults on moving the market to standalone status, with a decision due by the end of June 2027 [S24]. The direction of travel is toward less passive money, not more, and there is no dated event that forces the company to act [S25]. If that persists, the shares can remain at a discount to fundamental value for years, and the bear regime case value of Rp898 is the honest measure of that outcome [S22, S24].

The second risk is the commodity itself. The house agri deck assumes CPO rises from US$1,135/t to US$1,240/t before easing to US$1,150/t; the spot print is US$1,180/t and the archive shows prices falling to a twenty-five-week low in early November 2026 [S16]. A price that undershoots the deck cuts revenue and margin at the same time, because the purchased-feed leg of cost does not fall as fast as the selling price on the way down. Our bear business scenario prices CPO at the deck's own FY2023A trough of US$886/t and volume slightly lower, and even that produces a value of Rp646, below today's price. At that trough the model's EBITDA falls back toward the FY2023 level, the interest bill of IDR758.1bn absorbs most of it, and the payout would not be covered.

The third risk is the balance sheet. Net debt is 1.7x FY2026E EBITDA, which is manageable, but the current position is tighter than the annual average: current liabilities of IDR9,480.0bn against current assets of IDR11,100.0bn that include the IDR3,200.0bn restricted DHE balance [S7]. The dividend commitment of IDR500.0bn for FY2026 is large relative to the unrestricted retained earnings of IDR3,040.0bn, and the syndicated facility of IDR5,200.0bn carries security over group assets [S3, S13]. Under the FY2023 trough EBITDA of IDR1,136.3bn, the FY2026E dividend of Rp139 a share and capex of IDR731.5bn would not be covered, so a weak CPO year would force a choice between the payout and the capex programme, and the market would read that choice as a signal [S12, S7]. The 30 September 2026 net debt of IDR11,125.3bn against that trough EBITDA is close to ten times, far above the 6.2x struck on FY2023's own balance sheet, because the current balance sheet carries much more debt than the FY2023 one [S7, F101].

The fourth risk is governance and related-party dealing. The SML acquisition was an affiliate transaction with the 62.3% controlling shareholder, at a price of IDR1,600.0bn for a 63.4% stake, funded with debt raised by the listed company [S13, S5]. The seller retained 36.5%, so the group still owns the minority of the asset and participates in its upside, while the listed company carries the financing [S5]. That is not evidence of wrongdoing, but it is the structure through which value can move away from minority shareholders, and it is why we treat the IDR3,200.0bn restricted balance and the guarantee of the syndicated facility as governance items as much as accounting ones [S7, S4].

The operational risks are ordinary for the sector and concentrated by geography. All of the estates and mills are in Central Kalimantan, so a fire season, a flood or a mill outage hits the whole system at once; the company has publicly supported fire-suppression efforts in the province, which tells us the exposure is live [S16, S13]. A fifth of throughput comes from third-party growers, whose fruit supply is contested and whose quality drives the extraction rate [S11]. Weather also affects the young SML palms, whose contribution is the main volume assumption in the forecast [S4, S5].

Currency and rate risk sit alongside. Revenue is dollar-linked and costs are rupiah, so a stronger rupiah compresses the margin; the house macro deck (fund record) assumes the exchange rate drifts from Rp18,190/USD to Rp18,350/USD, and a reversal of that path would take several percent off the DCF [S0]. The debt is rupiah-denominated but the cost is not fixed: the model's 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt reflects current facility pricing, and a refinancing at a higher spread would hit the equity value directly [S13, S0].

The business scenarios are anchored to the observed cycle rather than to round-number haircuts. The bear case prices CPO at the deck's FY2023A trough, cuts volume by a twentieth as the SML ramp slips, and values the equity at Rp646. The base case holds the deck and gives Rp2,581. The bull case prices CPO a fifth above the deck, lifts volume by a twentieth as the young palms mature faster, and gives Rp3,890 [S4]. The probabilities are one quarter bear, one half base and one quarter bull, reflecting genuine uncertainty about the palm price rather than a cautious tilt. The asymmetry in the CPO shock is deliberate: the bear is the last observed trough, while the bull is a normal up-cycle, and the QC gate records the reason.

The konglo regime scenarios are a separate layer and they are what set the target. The business scenarios value the plantation; the regime scenarios decide how much of the gap between price and value survives twelve months [S22, S24]. The lens keeps a probability-weighted share of today's discount: the base case closes 25.0% of the log gap and gives Rp1,304, the bear case lets the discount widen by -20.0% of the log gap and gives Rp898, and the bull case closes 65.0% and gives Rp1,815. Weighted, that is our Rp1,330 target from the engine's konglo lens [S22, S24]. The regime layer is why a BUY target sits so far below our own DCF: we are not assuming the discount disappears. The target is also weight-dependent: with half the weight on the bear regime rather than a quarter, the weighted value falls but stays above the current price, so the BUY survives a materially more bearish regime view. The three-quarters weight on some closure is not a weight on full closure: the base regime closes only a quarter of the log gap and the bull most of it, so even the optimistic branch leaves a discount in place. The regime weights are the house konglo deck's, not ours, and we keep the symmetric one-quarter/one-half/one-quarter weights because the base case is the most likely single path and the group has shown willingness to simplify, but the reader should see the dependence.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. An announcement that the group will lift the public float, simplify the holding structure or seek index re-inclusion would move us toward the bull regime case [S22, S25]. A further affiliate transaction, a pledge of shares or a cut in the payout would move us toward the bear case [S13, S12]. A CPO print persistently below the house agri deck's US$1,150/t would lower fundamental value and make the discount arithmetic less forgiving. And a refinancing of the syndicated facility on better terms would reduce the balance-sheet risk that currently caps the multiple [S13].

Ownership is the defining fact. PT Citra Borneo Indah holds 62.3% of SSMS directly. The exchange's IDX-IC registry measures the free float at 29.2%, which is the regulator's own definition, the figure the minimum-float rule tests and the one that leaves the name compliant [S25, S0]. The pack also carries insider and institution fields, but they overlap rather than partition the register (they sum well above the whole alongside the registry float), so we do not treat them as a residual calculation; the residual after the controlling block is thinner than the registry number, and we use it only as a sensitivity [S0, S13]. The company sits inside the Citra Borneo Indah group, and the parent is both the controlling shareholder and the counterparty in the SML transaction, which is the classic related-party configuration in Indonesian plantations [S13, S5]. The board has three commissioners, of whom one is independent, and five directors including a dedicated sustainability director appointed at the October 2025 meeting [S4].

The market-structure overlay is now as important as the ownership itself. SSMS appears on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, a disclosure status that by itself is not a finding of wrongdoing [S22]. HSC names are excluded from the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026, which removes the index bid without delisting the shares [S26]. MSCI has frozen index increases for Indonesian securities and is consulting on a reclassification from emerging to standalone market status, with a final decision by the end of June 2027; the consultation cites persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading as reasons [S24]. The exchange has raised the minimum free float with a phased timetable; on the registry measure SSMS is above it, so no free-float step is due, but the residual after the controlling block is thin enough that the rule is a live constraint for the group rather than a non-event [S25, S0].

Related-party gravity is high. The SML purchase transferred IDR1,600.0bn from the listed company to its controlling shareholder for a 63.4% stake in an estate that CBI had held at 99.9%, leaving CBI with 36.5% of the asset and the listed company with the debt [S13, S5]. The acquisition was correctly classified as an affiliate transaction and approved by shareholders, and the price was supported by an appraisal, but the economics are still a transfer within the group rather than a market purchase [S13]. The syndicated facility of IDR5,200.0bn is secured by group assets and was approved at the same meeting that approved the acquisition, so the minority's balance sheet is pledged to a facility whose proceeds also funded the affiliate purchase [S4, S13].

On audit and disclosure, the archive is thinner than we would like. The company's investor-relations site returned a template page rather than a document library, the annual report we could retrieve is a scanned file with no extractable text, and the exchange's own filing portal refused automated access [S6]. We therefore could not verify the auditor's opinion, the related-party note or the segment note from a primary filing, and we flag that as an evidence gap rather than a finding [S6]. The financial figures in this report come from the archived press coverage of the audited FY2025 accounts and the nine-month FY2026 statements, which we cross-checked across three outlets [S8, S7, S2].

The dividend record is strong but short. The company paid Rp84 a share for FY2025, 68.9% of parent profit, after paying IDR800.0bn in total, and has declared a IDR500.0bn interim for FY2026 at Rp52 a share [S12, S3]. The payout is high for a cyclical producer and it is being paid while gross debt rises, which is a capital-allocation choice worth monitoring rather than a red flag on its own [S0, S7]. The unrestricted retained earnings balance of IDR3,040.0bn supports the current level but not an indefinite increase [S3].

ESG exposure is concentrated in land, traceability and smallholders. The company reports full ISPO certification across its operations and RSPO certification for its sustainability standard, with traceability across 2,000,000 t of FFB including 516,000 t from third parties [S11, S21]. It supports an independent smallholder association with 774 members and helped establish a village enterprise with 506 farmers, which is the social-licence work that matters most in a province where land conflicts are common [S11]. It runs a carbon-accounting programme and an orangutan conservation partnership with the Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation, and it participates in social-forestry schemes around its concessions [S11]. The main residual ESG risk is fire and haze, which is a regional exposure the company shares with every planter in Kalimantan and which it has publicly helped to fight [S16, S13].

The governance discount is therefore not a mystery. A controlling family, a related-party acquisition, a concentrated register, a thin independent board presence and an index regime that is moving against exactly this structure are the inputs the konglo lens is built to price [S22, S24]. We do not think the company is badly run; the operating record on OER, certification and traceability is better than the sector average [S14, S11]. We do think the minority shareholder is paid a discount for accepting the structure, and the valuation says that discount is currently very wide.

The dated catalysts are these. The interim dividend goes ex on 11 November 2026, with a record date of 12 November and payment on 2 December 2026, which puts IDR500.0bn into shareholders' hands before the year-end [S3]. The exchange reviews its high-shareholding-concentration list periodically, and any change to SSMS's status would be the single largest re-rating event available to the stock [S22]. MSCI's consultation runs to a final decision by the end of June 2027, with the freeze on index increases in place until then [S24]. The FY2026 audited accounts are due in April 2027, following the FY2025 publication on 1 April 2026, and they will be the first full year of SML consolidation [S10, S13]. The free-float timetable runs to 31 March 2028; SSMS is compliant on the registry measure, with the thin residual after the controlling block as the sensitivity, so it is a company catalyst as well as a peer one [S25].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the CPO price against the house agri deck's US$1,240/t and the realisation wedge against our 0.95 assumption; the quarterly extraction rate against the FY2025 22.1% [S14]; processed volume and the third-party share against the 516,000 t base, because a fall in purchased fruit would signal that the mill system is losing its supply franchise [S11]; the minority share of profit as SML seasons, because it determines how much of group growth reaches parent shareholders [S7]; net debt and the current ratio, with the IDR3,200.0bn restricted balance treated as unavailable [S7]; the payout against unrestricted retained earnings [S3]; and any change to the HSC list, the free float or the group's ownership structure [S22, S25].

The thesis is falsifiable on three points. If CPO holds below the house agri deck's US$1,150/t for a full cycle, the fundamental value falls toward the bear case and the discount is no longer wide enough to compensate. If the company makes another affiliate acquisition on debt-funded terms, the governance discount should widen rather than close [S13]. If the HSC status is lifted and the free float rises without a dilutive issuance, the lens's base compression is too low and the target is too conservative [S22, S25]. Each of those is observable within the next twelve months.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E CPO-equivalent sales of 1,045kt: the FY2025 revenue-implied volume was 941kt [F59], and SML (11,046 ha, young palms, completed 24 November 2025) consolidates for a full year, lifting own output and third-party throughput; 9M2026 revenue growth of 34.85% [S7] is consistent with that step-up on a higher CPO price and FX. Growth fades to 1.4%/yr by FY2030 as the young-planting uplift annualises, then volume is held flat.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: 0.95 of the CPO benchmark across the cycle, calibrated on the FY2025 actual: revenue of Rp14.81tn at the FY2025 benchmark of US$1,007/t and average FX of 16,448 implies a realised ASP of US$956.65/t, a 5% wedge to the deck. SSMS sells CPO plus RBD palm olein, crude palm kernel oil and palm kernel, which carry a small product premium, but bears the Indonesian export levy and duty plus freight; the wedge is held flat rather than assuming it narrows or widens. Volume and realisation are jointly identified from the revenue line, so the pair is anchored to the actual year rather than to a peer's product mix [S7][S10]. The archive carries no product-level revenue split and no levy schedule, so the wedge cannot be decomposed; a peer's lower realisation would require a different volume to reproduce the same revenue, and the calibration gate validates the EBITDA level rather than the split.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No price cap applies to palm oil; the domestic-market obligation is a sales-allocation rule, not a capped price.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Cost-intensity factor of 1.0: one tonne of CPO-equivalent sold consumes one unit of cost_per_bcm, so cost_per_bcm is the all-in cash cost per tonne and there is no separate mining ratio.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: FY2026 base cash cost of Rp10.44m/t, set so that the full unit cost at the FY2026 benchmark reproduces the 9M2026 actual of Rp10.75m/t: 9M2026 COGS of Rp8,890bn less D&A of Rp473bn is Rp8,417bn of cash cost on the 9M volume the revenue line implies, and the same run-rate carried through Q4 gives the full-year cost. The FY2025 base of Rp10.25m/t is superseded because it reproduced the FY2025 year, not the FY2026 run-rate; the 9M2026 cash cost is 1.8% above the old base after allowing for the purchased-feed pass-through. It grows 2.5%/yr with IDR inflation; the CPO-linked share is added by the fuel term, so the full unit cost rises with both inflation and the benchmark.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: 23.5% is the purchased-feed share of throughput: third-party FFB of 516kt plus plasma FFB of 44.4kt against 2,383kt processed [F19][F62][F6]. That is the share of the cost base whose price tracks the CPO benchmark, so the template's price-link term passes the benchmark through to that slice; the remaining 76.5% is own-estate cost that moves with inflation. The earlier 60% was not sourced to the physical purchased share and is withdrawn.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: all cash cost is carried in cost_per_bcm so the unit cost is not double counted.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: No mining-style royalty: the Indonesian CPO export levy and duty are embedded in the 0.95 realisation wedge and in cash cost, so a separate royalty line would double count.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: No separate other-revenue line is disclosed; the revenue build covers CPO, olein, CPKO and palm kernel.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: No other revenue, so the margin is not used.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Rp604k/t for FY2026. The cash-flow identity implies FY2025 D&A of about Rp568bn (CFO of Rp1,097bn less net profit of Rp1,203bn plus the Rp674bn working-capital build), or Rp604k per revenue-implied tonne; the data pack's Rp73bn depreciation line is the G&A-only figure and is not used. D&A grows with inflation as the asset base expands.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Rp700k/t for FY2026: FY2025 capex of Rp475bn on 941kt was Rp505k/t, lifted for SML development, replanting and mill/infrastructure spend funded by the Rp5.2tn syndicated facility [S13]; it grows with inflation.

assumptions.basis: No separately costed expansion project is disclosed; growth capex is carried in capex_unit.
